value.body: Cabin crew are responsible for passenger safety on board — evacuation drills, first aid, security checks — as well as in-flight service. Airlines hire them directly and run their own initial training under DGCA rules. Private academies offer preparation courses, but an academy certificate is not a requirement to be hired.

items.label: Minimum qualification
items.note: Some airlines ask for a degree or hotel-management qualification

items.label: Airline training
items.value: Initial safety and service training by the airline
items.note: Followed by recurrent training through the career

items.label: Domestic air passengers
items.note: A rough sense of the industry's scale

value.title: How you get in
value.body: Airlines advertise cabin crew openings and hold walk-in or online selection rounds: grooming and communication assessment, group discussion or interview, and a medical check. Each airline sets its own age, height, vision and swimming requirements and asks for a valid passport. Private academy courses are optional preparation.

value.title: At a glance
items: Work includes early, late and overnight duties, time away from home, and standing for long hours.
Hiring rises and falls with airline expansion; openings can come in bursts.
Common next steps are senior crew, cabin supervisor, trainer, or ground roles in airports and hospitality.
Academy fees vary widely; airlines do not require a particular academy.
